identification.summary: Storm-1982 is a Microsoft Threat Intelligence designation with origin listed as China; Microsoft's public naming mapping lists 'SneakyCheff' and 'UNK_SweetSpecter' as other names for it [S1]. No Microsoft narrative report on Storm-1982 was found in open search. The two other names resemble Cisco Talos's 'SneakyChef' (a Chinese-speaking actor using the SugarGh0st and SpiceRAT remote access trojans against government entities) [S3][S4] and Proofpoint's 'UNK_SweetSpecter' (SugarGh0st phishing of people tied to a US AI organization) [S5]. The mapping entry does not explain how Microsoft derived the overlap, so the profile below describes the vendor activity that the aliases point to, not Microsoft-confirmed findings [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Talos: SugarGh0st campaign likely began as early as August 2023 [S2][S3]. Palo Alto Unit 42 reported the overlapping Operation Diplomatic Specter activity as underway since at least late 2022 (as relayed by Talos coverage) [S4].
identification.notes: Vendor cluster boundaries differ and are kept separate here. (1) Talos SneakyChef: government-targeting campaign, SugarGh0st then SpiceRAT [S3]; Talos told press it is linked to Unit 42's Operation Diplomatic Specter [S4]. (2) Proofpoint UNK_SweetSpecter: May 2024 SugarGh0st campaign against fewer than ten individuals connected to one US AI organization; Proofpoint did not tie it to a known nation-state actor [S5]. (3) OpenAI 'SweetSpecter': suspected China-based adversary whose accounts OpenAI banned in October 2024; its spear-phishing carried SugarGh0st [S6]. Whether (2) and (3) are the same cluster as (1), and whether Microsoft's Storm-1982 covers all three, is not stated in the sources reviewed. Microsoft's spelling 'SneakyCheff' differs from Talos's 'SneakyChef' [S1][S3].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft's mapping lists China as the origin of Storm-1982 but gives no confidence statement or sponsor [S1]. Talos assessed with low confidence in November 2023 that the SugarGh0st operator was Chinese-speaking [S2], and with medium confidence in June 2024 that SneakyChef operators are likely Chinese-speaking [S3]. Talos has not attributed SneakyChef to a specific government [S4]. Proofpoint did not attribute UNK_SweetSpecter to a known nation-state actor [S5]. OpenAI stated its banned accounts likely belonged to a suspected China-based adversary, based on a credible source's assessment [S6].
attribution.basis: Talos cited language preferences in the code, use of Gh0st RAT variants, and target selection for the Chinese-speaking assessment [S3]. OpenAI's attribution rested on a credible source and its account-level observations [S6]. No government attribution (indictment, advisory or sanction) was found for this cluster.

objectives: Talos describes SneakyChef as an espionage campaign against government entities, mostly foreign ministries and embassies, using remote access trojans [S3][S4]. Proofpoint's UNK_SweetSpecter activity targeted people connected to a US AI organization; Proofpoint did not state a goal beyond the targeting pattern and noted the timing coincided with US-China tension over AI [S5]. Sponsor-level objectives are not established.

sectors: Government (foreign ministries and embassies, per decoy content) [S3][S4]
Artificial intelligence organizations and associated academia/industry/government personnel (US) [S5][S6]
regions: Uzbekistan and South Korea (initial SugarGh0st campaign) [S2]
EMEA and Asia, widened scope; Talos named Angola, India, Latvia, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, and others per coverage [S3][S4]
targeting.notes: Talos's country list derives partly from decoy-document content, so it indicates lure themes and is provisional [S3][S4]. Proofpoint saw fewer than ten targeted individuals tied to a single US AI organization [S5]. OpenAI reported spear-phishing of its own staff and said earlier SweetSpecter activity focused on political entities in the Middle East, Africa and Asia [S6][S7].

capabilities.summary: SugarGh0st is a customized variant of Gh0st RAT that Talos assessed with high confidence [S2]. Delivery in the Talos-observed campaign used LNK files inside RAR/self-extracting archives that launch VBS or JavaScript stages [S3]. In June 2024 Talos reported a second RAT, SpiceRAT, delivered by two chains, one starting from an LNK in a RAR archive and one from an HTA file; SpiceRAT is sideloaded through a legitimate Samsung RunHelp executable and a malicious DLL [S3][S4]. Proofpoint's May 2024 campaign used AI-themed emails from a free email account with a zip archive containing an LNK that launched a JavaScript dropper and SugarGh0st, and the command-and-control moved to a new domain during the campaign [S5]. OpenAI reported the SweetSpecter actor used its models for vulnerability research, scripting and phishing support, and said this gave no new capability beyond public resources; phishing emails posed as ChatGPT users and carried a zip with an LNK delivering SugarGh0st [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: SugarGh0st campaign against Uzbekistan and South Korea
campaigns.summary: Talos reported on 2023-11-30 a campaign likely started as early as August 2023 delivering the new SugarGh0st RAT, with evidence suggesting targeting of the Uzbekistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs and users in South Korea; Talos assessed low confidence that the operator was Chinese-speaking [S2].

campaigns.name: SugarGh0st phishing of US AI organization personnel (UNK_SweetSpecter)
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reported a small campaign aimed at fewer than ten individuals connected to a single leading US AI organization, using AI-themed lures, a zip/LNK/JavaScript chain and SugarGh0st; no nation-state attribution was made [S5].

campaigns.name: SneakyChef expansion and SpiceRAT
campaigns.summary: Talos named the actor SneakyChef, reported a wider target set across EMEA and Asia using scanned government documents as lures, introduced SpiceRAT, and confirmed linkage to Unit 42's Operation Diplomatic Specter; Talos assessed medium confidence that the operators are likely Chinese-speaking [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: SweetSpecter spear-phishing of OpenAI staff (reported with account bans, 2024-10)
campaigns.summary: OpenAI's report of 2024-10-01 said it banned accounts likely belonging to a suspected China-based adversary it tracks as SweetSpecter, which used its models for research and scripting. OpenAI said it learned in May 2024, from a credible source, that the adversary was sending spear-phishing emails with a SugarGh0st-bearing attachment to its employees; its security systems blocked the emails. The date field marks the report, not the phishing activity [S6][S7].

diamond.adversary: Storm-1982 per Microsoft, origin China, no sponsor stated [S1]. Related vendor clusters assessed as likely Chinese-speaking at low to medium confidence [S2][S3]; OpenAI says suspected China-based [S6].
diamond.capability: SugarGh0st (customized Gh0st RAT) and SpiceRAT; LNK/RAR/HTA/VBS/JavaScript delivery; DLL sideloading via a legitimate Samsung executable; AI-assisted research and scripting reported by OpenAI [S2][S3][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Proofpoint cited a command-and-control domain change to account.gommask[.]online during its campaign [S5]. Phishing used a free email account [S5]. Wider infrastructure detail was not retrieved.
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries and embassies themes and government entities in EMEA and Asia [S2][S3][S4]; personnel connected to a US AI organization, including OpenAI staff [S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Proofpoint noted the AI-organization targeting coincided with US-China tensions over AI access [S5]. Government-targeting lures follow foreign-ministry and embassy themes [S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached by email attachments (zip/RAR archives with LNK or HTA files); Gh0st-derived RATs [S3][S5].

gaps: No Microsoft report on Storm-1982 was found; the basis for Microsoft's mapping of SneakyCheff and UNK_SweetSpecter to it is unknown [S1].
Whether Talos SneakyChef, Proofpoint UNK_SweetSpecter and OpenAI SweetSpecter are one cluster is unconfirmed; Microsoft's mapping lists two of the names only [S1].
No government attribution or sponsor (MSS, PLA, contractor) identified.

Talos's original blog posts, the Proofpoint report and the OpenAI report could not be opened directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries and press coverage, so verify against primaries.
Unit 42 Operation Diplomatic Specter details were not reviewed; the link is relayed through Talos coverage [S4].
Activity after October 2024 was not found.
Full infrastructure and indicator set not collected.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: relevant battlespace is email-reachable Windows endpoints of foreign ministries, embassies and AI-sector personnel; civilian and allied government networks are the observed environment, not DoD networks [S3][S5]. Step 3 (adversary): a likely Chinese-speaking espionage actor using Gh0st-derived RATs and archive/LNK/HTA delivery [S2][S3]. Step 4, MLCOA: continued phishing with diplomatic or technology-themed lures delivering SugarGh0st/SpiceRAT-style RATs to government and AI-sector users [S3][S5][S6]. MDCOA: broader targeting of defense-adjacent research or contractor staff using AI-themed lures, with AI tools aiding scripting and phishing; this is inference from the OpenAI report [S6]. Candidate indicators: LNK-in-archive attachments, HTA droppers, Samsung RunHelp sideloading of an unsigned DLL, and AI-service-themed lures from free email accounts [S3][S5][S6]. Cluster identity is unresolved, so treat as a hypothesis set.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft, Talos, Proofpoint and OpenAI reporting separately and note the unresolved cluster mapping [S1][S3][S5][S6]. Authorities: observed targets are foreign and civilian entities; any defensive support to partners or defense-industrial-base owners follows existing DCO and information-sharing authorities, which the sources do not address. Mission assurance: prioritize email attachment filtering (archive, LNK, HTA), endpoint detection for DLL sideloading, and user awareness for personnel who work with AI or foreign-ministry counterparts [S3][S5]. Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs and industry via established channels; the cited material is open vendor reporting and indicators should be re-validated before action.
